sections.subtitle: The growth-pipeline and parent-leverage metrics behind the standalone DCF -- a secondary signal while the $15.00/share take-private is pending

charts.title: Renewables Backlog: Signed PPAs vs Under Construction

backlog.title: Renewables backlog
backlog.content:
Signed PPA backlog is contracted renewables capacity (GW) with a signed power purchase agreement but not yet in service -- the revenue-committed growth pipeline. Under construction is the subset of that backlog actually being built today.

For The AES Corporation: this pipeline (~12GW signed, ~5-6GW under construction) is the evidence behind the standalone DCF's capex and growth path -- the three years of negative owner FCF in the base case are this backlog being funded and built out. It is a secondary signal while the $15.00/share take-private is pending, since the deal price already caps realisable value, but it is what a holder owns if the deal breaks.

What to watch:

  • Under-construction GW growing as a share of the signed backlog (conversion pace)
  • Backlog additions outpacing cancellations/expirations
  • Tax-credit policy (2025 Act wind/solar phase-out, FEOC rules) governing which of this backlog remains economic

usRenewablesBacklog.title: US Clean Energy segment backlog
usRenewablesBacklog.content:
The AES Clean Energy segment's own cut of the signed renewables backlog -- US-only, a subset of the total PPA backlog chart.

For The AES Corporation: US projects sit inside the 2025 Act's domestic tax-credit and FEOC-restriction regime, so this line isolates the part of the pipeline most exposed to that policy, versus the Latin America/international backlog captured only in the total PPA figure.

What to watch:

  • Growth here versus growth in the total PPA backlog (US share of the pipeline)
  • Project economics as the investment tax credit phases out post-2027

parentLiquidityDebt.title: Parent-company liquidity and recourse debt
parentLiquidityDebt.content:
Parent-company liquidity is cash and committed facilities held at the AES Corporation parent, excluding project-level (non-recourse) cash. Recourse debt is debt the parent itself is obligated to repay, as distinct from non-recourse project debt that sits with individual plants and their partners.

For The AES Corporation: the standalone DCF's attributable net-debt bridge turns on splitting consolidated debt into recourse (the parent's problem) and non-recourse (partner-borne) -- the undisclosed split is a key valuation sensitivity (each 10pp of non-recourse debt is roughly $3.8/share). This chart is the parent-level liquidity and obligation an owner of AES equity, not a project partner, actually carries.

What to watch:

  • Parent liquidity falling while recourse debt rises (refinancing or covenant risk)
  • Recourse debt growth outpacing the backlog it is meant to fund

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For The AES Corporation: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For The AES Corporation: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For The AES Corporation: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For The AES Corporation: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For The AES Corporation: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For The AES Corporation: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For The AES Corporation: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For The AES Corporation: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For The AES Corporation: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
